name: GlyNAC

angle.text: Users take GlyNAC in longevity-minded appearance circles in the hope that restoring glutathione slows ageing and keeps skin looking younger. The small trials measured glutathione and ageing markers in older adults, not wrinkles or skin appearance, so the skin link is speculative.

summary: Glycine + NAC combo with small trials on glutathione and aging markers.
currentQuick:
GlyNAC is a combination of glycine and N-acetylcysteine proposed to restore glutathione levels that decline with age. It is sold as an over-the-counter supplement.
Small trials by one academic group in older adults reported improved glutathione, inflammation markers and some physical function measures. Sample sizes are small, and appearance effects have not been shown.
How it works: Cysteine (from NAC) and glycine are the two limiting amino acids for glutathione synthesis, so supplementing both is hypothesized to improve antioxidant capacity and mitochondrial function.
Risks and caveats: Adverse effects are mainly gastrointestinal, from NAC. Trial doses are large and long-term safety has not been established. Legal as a supplement.
deepLead:
GlyNAC is a combination of two amino acids, glycine and N-acetylcysteine (NAC, a precursor of cysteine), that are the building blocks limiting the body's synthesis of the antioxidant tripeptide glutathione. It is sold over the counter as a dietary supplement and has been studied mainly as an intervention for age-related glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction.
The concept was developed by Rajagopal Sekhar and colleagues at Baylor College of Medicine, whose group has published most of the human work on it, beginning with an open-label trial in older people with HIV in 2020 and a pilot trial in older adults in 2021. A randomized trial in older adults followed in 2023. The researchers report improvements in glutathione levels, inflammation markers, insulin resistance, muscle strength, cognition and body composition.
The published human trials are small, were largely run by one research group, and enrolled older adults rather than people seeking cosmetic changes. No study has examined effects on facial appearance, skin or other aesthetic outcomes, and reviews describe the evidence as promising but preliminary.

name: Alpha-ketoglutarate

angle.text: AKG is taken by people in longevity circles who hope slowing biological ageing will show up as younger skin and fewer wrinkles. Research is preliminary and focused on ageing markers; effects on visible skin ageing in people are untested.

summary: Metabolic intermediate investigated in aging biology. Preliminary.
currentQuick:
Alpha-ketoglutarate (AKG) is a key intermediate in the citric acid cycle and in amino acid metabolism. It is sold as a supplement, often as calcium AKG.
It attracted longevity interest after mouse studies showed extended lifespan and compressed morbidity. Human evidence is preliminary, with small, company-linked studies and no demonstrated cosmetic benefit.
How it works: AKG is a cofactor for dioxygenases involved in epigenetic regulation (such as TET enzymes and histone demethylases) and for collagen hydroxylation, and it links energy and nitrogen metabolism.
Risks and caveats: Generally regarded as well tolerated in short-term use, but long-term human safety data are limited. Legal as a supplement. Claims about reduced biological age come from small, non-definitive studies.
deepLead:
Alpha-ketoglutarate (AKG, also 2-oxoglutarate) is an organic acid that occurs naturally in the body as an intermediate of the citric acid cycle and as a hub linking energy metabolism with amino acid and nitrogen handling. It is also sold as an over-the-counter supplement, usually as a calcium salt, and has attracted interest in longevity circles.
Interest rose after a 2020 study reported that dietary calcium AKG extended lifespan and reduced frailty in ageing mice. Reviews of AKG as a human supplement note that the human literature is thin, consisting of a few older studies on muscle, wound healing and post-surgical recovery, with no recent published trials demonstrating effects on ageing or age-related disease.
No study has tested AKG for cosmetic or appearance outcomes. Wikipedia's article states there are currently no randomized controlled trials showing pharmacological effects of AKG in humans. Several trials in older or middle-aged adults are registered or ongoing.

name: Caffeine (topical)

angle.text: Users apply caffeine creams and serums under the eyes to reduce puffiness and dark circles, usually before photos or events. Vasoconstriction explains a short-lived effect; small studies exist for under-eye products, while claims about facial fat or body fat are anecdotal.

summary: Constricts vessels for a temporary under-eye depuff.
currentQuick:
Topical caffeine is included in many under-eye creams and serums intended to reduce puffiness and dark circles. It is the same xanthine alkaloid found in coffee and tea, used here at low concentrations in a cosmetic base.
The effect is cosmetic and temporary. Some small studies show reduced swelling and improved appearance, but the evidence is limited and often uses short follow-up and company-run designs.
How it works: Caffeine is a vasoconstrictor that narrows small vessels, which may reduce visible blood pooling and fluid in the thin periorbital skin. It may also act as an antioxidant and may promote lipolysis and drainage in tissue, although penetration through skin is modest and effects are short-lived.
Risks and caveats: Topical use is usually well tolerated, with occasional irritation or allergy. Product guidance generally advises avoiding contact with the eyes. Absorbed amounts are small, the evidence for product claims is limited, and the effect does not address structural causes of eye bags such as fat prolapse.
deepLead:
Topical caffeine refers to caffeine, the xanthine alkaloid found in coffee and tea, formulated at low concentrations in creams, serums and gels. It appears in many under-eye products marketed to reduce puffiness and dark circles.
Proponents and product marketing describe a temporary de-puffing effect attributed to narrowing of small blood vessels and to drainage of fluid from the thin skin around the eyes. The sources reviewed contain no controlled human trial of cosmetic caffeine products for under-eye puffiness or dark circles, so these effects have not been evaluated in the published literature reviewed here.
Published research on caffeine applied to the body surface is mostly pharmaceutical: studies of caffeine delivery through skin using lipid nanoparticle carriers, and animal and small human studies of caffeine eye drops for the lens and for intraocular pressure.

name: Hesperidin

angle.text: Hesperidin is a citrus flavonoid that users take hoping to improve under-eye circulation and reduce dark circles and puffiness. It has been studied for venous and capillary complaints in the legs, not under-eye appearance, so this use rests on extrapolation.

summary: Vein-supporting flavonoid used for venous and microvascular issues.
currentQuick:
Hesperidin is a flavanone glycoside concentrated in the peel of citrus fruits. It is sold as a supplement, often combined with diosmin in products used for chronic venous insufficiency and haemorrhoids.
In the context of facial puffiness and dark circles it is occasionally added to creams and supplements for its effects on small blood vessels. Evidence for periorbital use specifically is limited, and most clinical data concern venous disorders.
How it works: Hesperidin and its aglycone hesperetin are thought to improve vascular tone and capillary resistance, reduce microvascular permeability and dampen inflammation through antioxidant pathways. Oral bioavailability is low and depends on gut bacteria releasing the active aglycone.
Risks and caveats: Generally well tolerated, with mild gastrointestinal upset, headache or rash occasionally reported. It is recognised as safe as a food ingredient, but interactions with some medications that are metabolised by the liver are possible, and evidence for cosmetic claims is limited.
deepLead:
Hesperidin is a flavanone glycoside found in citrus fruits, concentrated in the white inner peel; its aglycone is hesperetin. It was first isolated in 1828 by the French chemist M. Lebreton. It is sold as a dietary supplement, often combined with diosmin or vitamin C, in products aimed at venous and capillary complaints.
In appearance communities it is discussed in the context of puffiness and dark circles, based on the idea that it supports small blood vessels. The sources reviewed contain no trial of hesperidin for periorbital puffiness or dark circles; the clinical literature concerns venous, metabolic and other conditions, and Wikipedia describes research on hesperidin as preliminary, with reviews finding no clear effect on blood lipids or blood pressure and inconclusive results on endothelial function.

name: Dandelion extract

angle.text: Users take dandelion tea or extract as a herbal diuretic to shed water weight and reduce facial puffiness, sometimes before a shoot or event. Evidence for a meaningful diuretic effect in people is weak and limited to small studies; appearance outcomes are untested.

summary: Marketed herbal diuretic. Weak evidence.
currentQuick:
Dandelion extract comes from the leaves or roots of Taraxacum officinale and is traditionally used as a mild herbal diuretic and digestive aid. It is sold as tea, capsules and tinctures.
In the appearance space it is marketed for "water weight" and facial bloating. Human evidence for a meaningful diuretic effect is very limited, so the claimed benefit for face depuffing is not supported by published human studies.
How it works: Dandelion leaf contains potassium and compounds that may promote modest urine output in animal studies, and the root contains inulin and sesquiterpene lactones. A small pilot study reported a short-lived increase in urination, but this is not strong evidence of a clinically significant effect.
Risks and caveats: Allergic reactions can occur in people sensitive to the daisy family (Asteraceae), including ragweed. It may interact with diuretics, lithium, anticoagulants and some antibiotics, and could raise potassium in susceptible people. Quality of herbal products varies.
deepLead:
Dandelion extract is a preparation from the leaves, roots or flowers of Taraxacum officinale, the common dandelion, a perennial of the daisy family (Asteraceae) native to Eurasia. The leaves, flowers and roots are used as food and in herbal medicine, and extracts are sold as teas, capsules and tinctures.
The plant has a long reputation as a diuretic. Wikipedia notes that this property is attributed to its high potassium content, that the leaves have been used as a diuretic in traditional Chinese medicine for roughly 2,000 years, and that French and English folk names ('pissenlit', 'piss-a-bed') refer to it. A 2009 study described 'promising' results while calling for further research. In appearance communities it is discussed as a way to reduce 'water weight' and facial bloating.
No published trial has tested dandelion extract for facial puffiness. Most laboratory research in the sources reviewed concerns antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer and animal-nutrition effects in cells and animals rather than humans.

name: Potassium

angle.text: Looksmaxxers raise potassium intake, usually through food, to offset sodium and reduce water retention and facial bloat. Potassium's role in fluid balance is well established, but whether it changes facial puffiness has not been directly studied; forum claims about ratios and powders are anecdotal.

summary: Electrolyte balance — fix the diet (and sodium) before buying pills.
currentQuick:
Potassium is an essential electrolyte that governs fluid balance, nerve signalling and muscle contraction, and is abundant in fruit, vegetables, legumes and dairy. Most people get it from food rather than supplements.
In depuffing discussions it is mentioned because a higher potassium-to-sodium balance supports normal fluid regulation. Reducing a high-sodium diet is described as more relevant than taking supplements, and evidence for facial de-bloating from potassium supplements is limited.
How it works: Potassium is the main intracellular cation. It works with sodium and the kidney to set extracellular fluid volume, and higher potassium intake promotes sodium excretion and lowers blood pressure. The face may look less puffy when overall fluid retention falls, though many causes of facial puffiness are unrelated to electrolytes.
Risks and caveats: Over-the-counter potassium supplements are limited in dose because excess can cause dangerous hyperkalaemia and heart rhythm problems, particularly in people with kidney disease or taking ACE inhibitors, ARBs or potassium-sparing diuretics. Dose limits and medical advice apply regardless of cosmetic purpose.
deepLead:
Potassium is an essential mineral and the main positively charged ion (cation) inside cells. It supports nerve signalling, muscle and heart contraction, and the maintenance of fluid balance and normal kidney function. It is obtained from foods such as potatoes, beans, fruit and dairy, and is also sold as supplements and as potassium chloride medicines.
In looksmaxxing and depuffing discussions, potassium is mentioned because the balance between sodium and potassium influences how the body handles fluid. Higher potassium intake promotes sodium excretion and has been found to lower blood pressure in trials. No published trial in the sources reviewed has tested potassium intake or supplements for facial puffiness.
Excess potassium (hyperkalaemia) is dangerous, and reviews and trials describe it in the context of kidney disease and drugs that raise potassium.

name: Furosemide

angle.text: Some users misuse this prescription diuretic off-label to drop water weight for a leaner or less puffy look before events or photos. It is studied for oedema, not cosmetic use; the effect is fluid loss rather than fat loss, and the appearance use is based on anecdote.

summary: Powerful medical loop diuretic.
note: Strong medically — dangerous and pointless as a cosmetic face-slimming trick.
currentQuick:
Furosemide (Lasix) is a potent loop diuretic used to treat fluid overload from heart failure, kidney disease and cirrhosis, and sometimes high blood pressure. It is prescription-only in nearly all countries.
It turns up in appearance and bodybuilding circles as a way to drop water weight quickly. Any resulting change in facial appearance reflects temporary fluid loss rather than loss of fat or bone, and misuse carries serious risks.
How it works: Furosemide blocks the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, so the kidney excretes more sodium, chloride, potassium and water. Onset is quick and the effect is strong, which makes electrolyte disturbances easy to cause.
Risks and caveats: Misuse can cause dehydration, low potassium, sodium and magnesium, cramps, dizziness, kidney injury, hearing damage and dangerous heart rhythms. It can interact with many drugs and is contraindicated in anuria and sulfonamide hypersensitivity. Use without medical supervision for cosmetic purposes is associated with these risks, and the drug is prohibited in many sports.
deepLead:
Furosemide, sold under the brand name Lasix among others, is a prescription loop diuretic used to treat oedema from heart failure, liver scarring (cirrhosis) and kidney disease, and sometimes high blood pressure. It was patented in 1959 and approved for medical use in 1964, is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines, and was the 29th most prescribed drug in the United States in 2023.
Furosemide acts within about an hour by mouth and within minutes by injection, causing the kidney to excrete large amounts of sodium, chloride, potassium and water. The US label carries a prominent warning that it is a potent diuretic which, if given in excessive amounts, can lead to profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion, and that careful medical supervision is required.
In bodybuilding and physique communities furosemide is discussed as a way of dropping water weight, and it is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's banned list because it may mask other drugs. No trial in the sources reviewed has examined it for cosmetic facial slimming or depuffing; its clinical evidence base concerns patients with fluid overload.

name: Whitening strips

angle.text: Users apply peroxide strips to lighten tooth colour for a brighter smile, often as the first whitening step. Peroxide bleaching is well studied for whitening; forum debates concern sensitivity, gum effects and non-peroxide or charcoal alternatives, which have less evidence.

summary: Peroxide bleaching that actually lifts tooth discoloration. ADA-backed, highest-confidence cosmetic buy.
currentQuick:
Whitening strips are thin, flexible plastic films coated with a peroxide gel, typically hydrogen peroxide at roughly 6 to 14 percent, that are pressed onto the front teeth for a set time each day over one to several weeks. They are sold over the counter and are the most widely used consumer route to lighter teeth.
In appearance terms they target extrinsic and mild intrinsic discoloration from coffee, tea, wine and age, and are generally regarded as one of the lower-cost and better-supported cosmetic options for the smile. Results fade gradually, and many users repeat short touch-up courses.
How it works: Hydrogen peroxide diffuses through enamel and breaks down into reactive oxygen species that cleave the large pigmented molecules lodged in the tooth, converting them into smaller, less colored fragments. The strip holds the gel against the tooth surface so the peroxide stays in contact long enough to act.
Risks and caveats: The main side effects are transient tooth sensitivity and gum irritation, usually mild and resolving after stopping. Strips cover mostly the front teeth and fit unevenly on crowded or irregular teeth, so coverage can be patchy. The Cochrane review of home bleaching rated much of the evidence as low certainty, while reporting that peroxide whitening itself is consistently shown to lighten teeth. Dental guidance generally advises seeking dental advice before overuse, or before whitening over untreated decay or exposed roots.
deepLead:
Whitening strips are thin, flexible plastic films coated with a peroxide gel that are pressed onto the front surfaces of the teeth for a set period, typically daily over one to several weeks, to lighten tooth colour. They are sold over the counter and are among the most widely used consumer tooth-whitening products.
Peroxide bleaching works by delivering hydrogen peroxide (directly or from carbamide peroxide) that diffuses into the tooth and breaks down into reactive species that fragment pigment molecules, so that they reflect less colour. Wikipedia reports that strips, introduced in the late 1980s, are typically applied twice daily for 30 minutes for 14 days and can lighten teeth by one or two shades within several days, depending on frequency of use and product.
Reviews describe peroxide-based whitening as safe and effective when manufacturers' protocols are followed, with transient tooth sensitivity and gum irritation as the main side effects. Randomized trials dating from 1992 onward have compared peroxide whiteners with placebo.

name: Whitening gel trays

angle.text: Users wear gel trays, custom or over-the-counter, to whiten teeth with peroxide, with posters claiming more even coverage than strips. Peroxide whitening is well studied; direct comparisons of tray types and long-term enamel effects are less certain, and forum claims vary.

summary: More even peroxide coverage than strips; dentist-fitted trays are the top tier.
currentQuick:
Whitening gel trays are soft plastic trays loaded with a carbamide or hydrogen peroxide gel and worn over the teeth for minutes to hours at a time. They come as custom-fitted trays made by a dentist from impressions or scans, or as boil-and-bite and prefilled over-the-counter versions.
Because the tray holds gel against every tooth surface, coverage is more even than with strips, and dentist-supervised take-home bleaching is regarded as a standard cosmetic dental option.
How it works: Carbamide peroxide breaks down into hydrogen peroxide and urea, and the released peroxide oxidizes pigment molecules inside enamel and dentin. A well-fitted tray keeps gel in constant contact with the teeth and away from the gums, allowing longer, lower-concentration exposure.
Risks and caveats: Tooth sensitivity and gum irritation are the common effects and are typically temporary; poorly fitting trays let gel leak onto the gums. A meta-analysis found tray carbamide peroxide and hydrogen peroxide systems comparable overall, and supervised trays give slightly larger measured color change than strips, though the difference may not be visible. Ill-fitting low-cost trays lose much of the coverage advantage, and a dental check beforehand is commonly recommended.
deepLead:
Whitening gel trays are flexible plastic trays that hold a peroxide-based bleaching gel against the teeth, usually for a period of minutes to hours or overnight. They are available as custom-fitted trays made by a dentist from impressions or digital scans, and as over-the-counter boil-and-bite or prefilled versions. The active ingredient is hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide, which releases hydrogen peroxide on contact with water. 
The hydrogen peroxide that is released diffuses into the tooth and breaks down pigmented organic molecules into smaller, less strongly coloured fragments, which makes the tooth reflect more light and appear whiter.  Because the tray keeps gel in contact with the tooth surfaces and, when well fitted, away from the gums, tray-based bleaching is one of the standard take-home options in dentistry. 
Clinical trials of tray bleaching with carbamide peroxide and hydrogen peroxide report measurable colour change on spectrophotometers, and the main adverse effects are tooth sensitivity and gum irritation, which are generally reported as temporary.  A scoping review of over-the-counter bleaching products noted that evidence for whitening strips comes mostly from clinical trials, whereas evidence for over-the-counter trays comes mainly from laboratory studies.  In looksmaxxing and fitness forums, trays are usually discussed as a cheaper alternative to strips or in-office treatment, often with a dentist-made custom tray as the preferred version.

name: LED whitening kit

chain: Peroxide gel plus blue LED light
angle.text: Users buy LED whitening kits as a home version of in-office light-assisted whitening, hoping the light speeds or boosts results. The peroxide gel is the studied active ingredient; evidence that the LED adds anything is limited.

summary: The peroxide does the work.
note: The blue light adds little beyond the gel alone.
currentQuick:
An LED whitening kit combines a peroxide gel, applied by tray, strip or pen, with a small mouthpiece that shines blue or violet LED light on the teeth. It is marketed as a salon-style treatment for home use.
The gel is the active whitening agent. The light accessory is the distinguishing feature, and it is the component with the least research support.
How it works: Peroxide gel bleaches by oxidizing stain molecules. The LED is claimed to speed gel breakdown, but the low-power lights in consumer kits deliver little energy, and studies of light activation in professional bleaching find no consistent extra whitening compared with gel alone.
Risks and caveats: Risks are those of the gel: sensitivity and gum irritation. Umbrella reviews report that light or laser activation does not reliably improve whitening and may increase sensitivity if poorly controlled. A narrow signal exists for violet light combined with carbamide peroxide, but the supporting evidence is limited and was tested in professional settings.
deepLead:
An LED whitening kit is a consumer tooth-whitening product that pairs a peroxide-based gel, applied by tray, strip or pen, with a small mouthpiece or handheld unit that shines blue or violet light-emitting-diode light on the teeth. Kits are sold over the counter as a home version of the light-assisted treatments offered in dental offices. 
The gel is the bleaching agent: hydrogen peroxide, or carbamide peroxide which releases it, oxidises pigmented molecules in the tooth.  The light component is the distinguishing feature of these kits, and its contribution has been tested mostly in professional in-office bleaching rather than in the low-power consumer devices. A systematic review and meta-analysis of in-office bleaching with versus without light, and two 2026 umbrella reviews on light and laser activation, have addressed the question, and a 2006 split-arch randomized study found no benefit from light over a chemically activated system after two weeks. 
Wikipedia reports that light-accelerated bleaching can enhance whitening when used properly but may increase sensitivity or add nothing when used improperly, and cites a 2015 study reporting that light activation did not improve bleaching and was likely to raise tooth temperature.  A small number of laboratory and clinical studies have looked specifically at LED-assisted whitening, including effects on ceramic restorations and on the gums.

name: Electric toothbrush

angle.text: Users switch to electric brushes for cleaner, healthier-looking teeth and gums and fresher breath. Powered brushes are studied for plaque and gum health; whitening claims are mostly about reducing surface stain and are less well supported.

summary: Better plaque removal and gum health than manual brushing.
currentQuick:
An electric or powered toothbrush uses a motor to drive the brush head in oscillating-rotating, sonic or other high-frequency motions. Many models add pressure sensors and timers to guide a two-minute brushing routine.
For appearance, the practical gains cited are cleaner teeth, less stain-trapping plaque and healthier gums, which together support a brighter, fresher-looking smile.
How it works: The motorized head performs thousands of strokes per minute, which removes plaque more consistently than many people manage by hand, and built-in timers and pressure alerts improve technique. Sonic models also create fluid movement around the bristles.
Risks and caveats: Side effects are rare and minor, mainly gum abrasion if pressed too hard. The large Cochrane review found modest advantages for powered brushes in plaque (about 11 to 21 percent) and gingivitis (about 6 to 11 percent), with the authors noting the clinical importance is uncertain. Manufacturers' premium claims often exceed that evidence, and mid-priced oscillating models are reported to perform similarly.
deepLead:
An electric or powered toothbrush uses a motor, or in some designs a piezoelectric crystal, to move the bristles in rapid oscillating, rotating, sonic or ultrasonic motions in place of the hand movements of a manual brush. Wikipedia classifies the devices by movement frequency as power, sonic or ultrasonic, and also by movement type, such as side-to-side vibration or oscillating-rotating heads.  Many current models add timers, pressure sensors, multiple cleaning modes and Bluetooth connectivity to a companion app. 
Powered brushes are used primarily for plaque control and gum health. For appearance, the relevance discussed in forums and marketing is that cleaner teeth carry less stain-trapping plaque and that healthier gums are associated with a fresher-looking smile; whitening modes are also offered on some models.  A Cochrane review of powered versus manual brushes found that powered brushes reduced plaque and gingival inflammation to a modest degree, with Wikipedia reporting reductions of about 11 percent and 6 percent after one to three months and 21 percent and 11 percent after three months, while noting that the clinical importance of the differences is debated. 
Among powered designs, the oscillating-rotating type is the one that Wikipedia says consistently showed a statistically significant advantage over manual brushing in the 2014 Cochrane review.  Reviews and trials have also examined children, orthodontic patients, elderly people and people with limited dexterity.

name: Water flosser

angle.text: Users add water flossers to clean between teeth and keep gums healthy so the smile looks better and breath is fresher. Studies have examined gum bleeding and plaque; comparisons with string floss and safety concerns are debated on forums.

summary: Interdental cleaning and gum health — healthy gums frame the smile.
currentQuick:
A water flosser, or oral irrigator, shoots a pulsing jet of water between teeth and along the gumline to flush out plaque and food debris. Countertop and cordless handheld versions are sold under brands such as Waterpik.
In appearance terms it is chiefly a gum-health tool, used by people with braces, implants or bridges, or who find string floss hard to use.
How it works: Pulsed water pressure dislodges loosely attached plaque and bacteria from interdental spaces and shallow pockets, and the massaging action is thought to reduce gingival inflammation and bleeding.
Risks and caveats: Safety is good; excessive pressure can bruise gums and it is not recommended straight after oral surgery. Systematic reviews show reliable improvements in gingival inflammation but inconsistent effects on plaque, and a recent meta-analysis found no extra benefit over regular floss for general patients. Many supporting trials are industry funded, and water flossers are generally described as an alternative to floss rather than a clear improvement on it.
deepLead:
A water flosser, also called an oral irrigator or dental water jet, is a home dental device that directs a pulsating stream of water at the teeth and gumline to flush plaque and food debris from between teeth and below the gum margin. The best-known maker, Waterpik, has become a generic name for the category. Countertop units with a reservoir and cordless rechargeable handhelds are both sold, with tips designed for braces, implants and bridges. 
Water flossers are used chiefly for gum health and interdental cleaning rather than for any direct cosmetic effect; their relevance to appearance is that gum inflammation and plaque affect the look of the gumline and breath. Wikipedia says regular use is believed to improve gingival health, and that more research is needed to confirm plaque biofilm removal and effects in patients with special needs. 
Systematic reviews report consistent reductions in gingival inflammation and bleeding with irrigation, with plaque results that vary between reviews; a 2008 review cited by Wikipedia found improved gingival health but no plaque reduction, while a 2023 systematic review of seven randomized trials in adults found most trials favoured water flossers over string floss for plaque reduction.  A literature review of safety concluded that decades of use and study support safety.  Many of the clinical trials are manufacturer-supported, and some dentists view irrigators as a supplement rather than a replacement for brushing and flossing.

name: Tongue scraper

angle.text: Users scrape the tongue to reduce coating and bad breath, which matters for close-up social presence. Studies show a short-lived reduction in breath odour and tongue coating; claims about the oral microbiome or diet-related breath are mostly anecdotal.

summary: Removes tongue coating; fresher breath for a few hours.
currentQuick:
A tongue scraper is a thin curved strip of metal or plastic drawn across the surface of the tongue to remove the whitish coating of bacteria, food debris and dead cells. The practice has long historical roots, including in Ayurvedic tradition.
It is used to reduce bad breath and keep the mouth feeling clean, which users link to social confidence and close-range appearance.
How it works: Most oral malodor comes from sulfur compounds produced by bacteria that colonize the rough tongue dorsum. Scraping physically removes the coating and the bacteria and substrates within it, lowering volatile sulfur compounds for a period.
Risks and caveats: Side effects are minor: gagging, soreness or occasional bleeding if scraped too hard. Cochrane and later reviews found a small short-term reduction in breath compounds compared with toothbrushing, based on very small trials, and insufficient evidence for chronic halitosis. Dental guidance is that breath that stays bad despite cleaning warrants a dental or medical check for gum disease or other causes.
deepLead:
A tongue scraper, also called a tongue cleaner, is a small hand tool, typically a curved strip or loop of metal or plastic, drawn along the top surface of the tongue to remove the coating of bacteria, food debris and shed cells that can build up there. Tongue brushes and brush-backed toothbrush heads serve a similar purpose.  Tongue cleaning is less commonly practised than tooth brushing, flossing or mouthwash use. 
It is used mainly to reduce oral malodour (bad breath) and to lessen the white or coloured tongue coating, which Wikipedia says can result from diet, reduced saliva flow, poor oral hygiene or tongue anatomy.  The practice has a long history, including in Ayurvedic tradition, where metal scrapers were used. 
A 2006 Cochrane review of tongue scraping for halitosis included two trials with 40 participants in total and reported a statistically significant short-term reduction in volatile sulfur compounds with scrapers, but the data could not be pooled and the evidence was described as limited.  Later reviews reported small short-term effects relative to toothbrushing, with little evidence on medium-term or chronic halitosis.  Wikipedia states that there are no clear scientific conclusions on its benefit for bad breath.

name: Clear aligners

angle.text: Users wear clear aligners to straighten teeth and correct bite, and some hope for subtle facial-structure benefits such as palate width. Tooth movement is well studied; claims about jaw or facial-skeleton change are limited and debated, and larger skeletal problems are generally described as needing other treatment.

summary: Actually moves teeth and fixes bite in suitable cases.
note: Dentist territory — not a DIY purchase.
currentQuick:
Clear aligners are a series of removable, transparent plastic trays, each shaped slightly differently, that gradually move teeth toward a planned position. Brands include Invisalign and a range of dentist-supervised and direct-to-consumer systems.
They are used to straighten crooked or crowded teeth, close gaps and correct some bite problems, with the added appeal of being nearly invisible compared with metal braces.
How it works: Each tray is thermoformed from a digital treatment plan and applies light, controlled force that remodels the bone around the tooth root. Bonded composite attachments give the plastic grip to produce movements like rotation, and trays are typically changed every one to two weeks.
Risks and caveats: Reviews show aligners work well for mild to moderate alignment, leveling and some intrusion, but are less predictable for rotations, extrusion and root control, especially in extraction cases. Risks include gum recession, root resorption, relapse without retainers, and poor outcomes when worn too little. A dentist or orthodontist confirms suitability, and mail-order and DIY versions omit that safeguard.
deepLead:
Clear aligners are removable, transparent plastic orthodontic appliances that move teeth in small steps through a series of trays, each shaped slightly differently from the last. A digital scan or impression of the teeth is used to plan the movements in software, and a new aligner is typically worn for one to two weeks and for about 22 hours a day.  Align Technology's Invisalign, which began US sales in 1999, is the best-known system; many other brands, including dentist-supervised and direct-to-consumer services, now exist. 
Aligners are used to straighten crowded or spaced teeth and to correct some bite problems, with the appeal that they are far less visible than metal braces and can be removed for eating and cleaning.  Wikipedia describes them as indicated mainly for mild to moderate crowding or spacing of roughly 1 to 6 mm in cases without jaw discrepancies, and as likely less effective than conventional braces for some movements such as rotations and tooth-position changes. 
The scientific literature includes several systematic reviews, and their conclusions are qualified. A 2015 systematic review identified methodological shortcomings in the available studies, and later reviews and meta-analyses compare aligners with fixed appliances across malocclusion types and in extraction cases. name: Bruxism night guard

chain: Less tooth wear and jaw strain
angle.text: Users wear night guards to stop grinding from flattening teeth and to ease jaw strain, which they link to keeping teeth and facial symmetry intact. Splints are studied for protecting teeth; effects on facial appearance are untested.

summary: Stops grinding from flattening your teeth over the years.
currentQuick:
A bruxism night guard, or occlusal splint, is a hard or soft plastic appliance worn over the teeth during sleep to protect them from grinding and clenching. Custom guards are made by a dentist, while stock and boil-and-bite versions are sold over the counter.
It is used to prevent enamel wear, chipping and flattening of teeth, which over years can change how the smile looks.
How it works: The guard places a plastic barrier between the upper and lower teeth so grinding forces wear the appliance instead of the enamel. It does not stop the underlying muscle activity, which is linked to stress, sleep arousals and other factors.
Risks and caveats: Splints are widely used and generally safe, but reviews find little direct evidence that they reduce tooth wear, and insufficient evidence that they cure bruxism itself; some designs may increase clenching or cause bite changes with full-time use. Ill-fitting or hard stock guards can be uncomfortable. Dental guidance is that a dentist assess for sleep apnea and other drivers.
deepLead:
A bruxism night guard, also called an occlusal splint, bite guard or nightguard, is a removable hard or soft plastic appliance worn over the teeth, usually at night, intended to protect them from the effects of grinding and clenching. Dentists make custom versions from impressions or scans, while stock and boil-and-bite versions are sold over the counter. 
Bruxism is defined in Grokipedia, citing a 2024 international consensus, as repetitive jaw-muscle activity involving clenching, grinding, or bracing of the mandible during sleep or wakefulness, and the consensus is described as treating it as a behaviour on a continuum rather than a disorder unless it causes harm such as dental damage or pain.  Occlusal splints and mouthguards are described there as a first-line measure to protect teeth.  For appearance, the interest in night guards is that long-term grinding can flatten, chip or wear teeth and change the look of the smile. 
Researchers have examined whether splints reduce bruxism itself, protect against wear or help temporomandibular symptoms. Systematic reviews of occlusal splints for bruxism and for temporomandibular disorder have been published, with authors generally noting that the quality and amount of evidence is limited and that the appliance is a protective device that does not remove the underlying muscle activity.  Wear of splint materials has been the subject of its own systematic review.

name: Jaw exerciser

angle.text: Users chew against silicone devices hoping for a sharper jawline and reduced double chin. The masseter can be trained, but forum posters note bigger muscles may widen the lower face; effects on definition or chin fat are largely untested.

summary: Works the chewing muscles, sure — but bigger masseters make the lower face wider, not sharper.
note: Overuse can aggravate TMJ. The marketing outruns the anatomy.
currentQuick:
A jaw exerciser is a silicone or plastic device, often a ball or resistance trainer, that the user bites or chews against to work the masseter and related chewing muscles. It is promoted on social media for a sharper, more defined jawline.
The devices sit in the looksmaxxing space alongside hard gum and chewing routines, where bigger jaw muscles are assumed to produce better jaw definition.
How it works: Resistance chewing loads the masseter and temporalis, which can increase muscle stiffness, endurance and in some cases size. Muscle growth widens the lower face at the angle of the jaw rather than removing fat or changing bone structure.
Risks and caveats: No controlled trial has shown that the devices improve jawline definition; the available literature consists of small studies on muscle stiffness and a two-person case report finding no change in the jawline or double chin. Overuse can strain the temporomandibular joint and cause jaw pain, headaches and tooth wear. People with TMJ symptoms are generally advised to avoid them.
deepLead:
A jaw exerciser is a handheld or mouth-worn resistance device, usually made of silicone or plastic and often shaped like a ball, bar or pair of plates, that the user bites or chews against to train the muscles of mastication, chiefly the masseter. Products in this category are sold under names such as Jawzrsize and are promoted on social media for a more defined jawline and reduced double chin.  The same term and similar devices also exist in clinical practice, where jaw exercisers are used in rehabilitation of restricted mouth opening. 
The masseter is a thick muscle that raises the lower jaw and attaches at the angle of the mandible. Wikipedia reports that the muscle can enlarge in people who habitually clench or grind their teeth and in those who constantly chew gum, and that this enlargement is generally soft and painless.  The idea behind cosmetic jaw exercisers is that a larger masseter will change the appearance of the lower face. 
A 2024 case report of two people who used a commercial jaw exerciser for about three months found no noticeable changes in jaw appearance, and its authors reported that a review of the literature found limited evidence that these devices reduce double chins, enhance jawlines or tighten facial skin, noting that the mastication muscles do not directly affect submental fat or skin elasticity.  No controlled trial of cosmetic jaw exercisers on jawline definition was found. Studies on masticatory muscle stiffness and oxygen dynamics after chewing

name: Mastic / hard gum

angle.text: Users chew mastic or hard gum to give the jaw muscles resistance work in hope of a more defined jawline. Jaw-muscle growth from chewing is plausible, but evidence for jawline appearance is anecdotal, and posters also raise joint-strain concerns.

summary: Masseter workout in gum form. Jawline effects uncertain, same width-vs-definition problem.
currentQuick:
Mastic gum is a hard, chewy resin from the mastic tree (Pistacia lentiscus) grown mainly on the Greek island of Chios, and it is marketed alongside harder-than-normal gums such as Turkish falim as a jaw-training gum. Several brands now sell mastic-based jawline gum.
It is used in looksmaxxing circles as a food-based way to work the masseter and encourage a more defined lower face.
How it works: Prolonged hard chewing makes the masseter and temporalis work against resistance, which may raise muscle stiffness, endurance and possibly size over time. The resin itself has traditional digestive uses, but any jaw effect is attributed to the chewing load, not the substance.
Risks and caveats: No controlled study shows mastic gum sculpts the jawline; small studies cover muscle stiffness and oxygen dynamics, not definition. Heavy chewing is associated with jaw muscle pain, TMJ strain and uneven wear, and larger masseters broaden rather than sharpen the face. Forum users themselves raise TMJ concerns, and the jawline effect is unproven.
deepLead:
Mastic gum is a chewable resin obtained from the mastic tree (Pistacia lentiscus var. chia), cultivated mainly on the southern part of the Greek island of Chios, and it is also the base of several commercial chewing gums. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed, together with other firm or long-lasting gums such as Turkish-style hard gum and branded 'jawline' gums, as a way to give the jaw muscles resistance training in the hope of a more defined lower face.
The resin itself has a long history in Mediterranean traditional medicine, particularly for digestive complaints, and has been examined in small clinical trials for stomach and duodenal conditions. Those studies concern digestive and other health outcomes, not facial appearance.
No published controlled study has tested whether chewing mastic or other hard gum changes jaw shape or facial definition in healthy adults. Related research is limited to short-term measurements of masseter muscle stiffness and oxygen dynamics after chewing, and to epidemiological work on gum chewing and temporomandibular disorder.

name: Mouth tape

angle.text: Users tape their mouths at night to encourage nasal breathing, claiming better sleep, fresher breath and in some forums forward jaw and midface development. Sleep and snoring effects have limited study; claims of adult facial-bone remodelling are unsupported.

summary: Encourages nasal breathing at night. Adult jaw remodeling claims: unsupported.
note: Risky if you have undiagnosed sleep apnea — rule that out first.
currentQuick:
Mouth taping means placing a strip of gentle tape over the lips at night to keep the mouth closed and encourage nasal breathing. It spread through social media with claims of better sleep, less snoring, fresher breath and a better jawline.
In looksmaxxing circles it is tied to the idea that nasal breathing shapes adult facial structure, a claim for which no supporting evidence has been published.
How it works: Sealing the lips forces air through the nose, which filters and humidifies it and may reduce dry mouth. Any effect on jaw shape has not been established, because adult facial bone does not meaningfully remodel with breathing route.
Risks and caveats: Systematic and scoping reviews find only small, preliminary studies, with one small trial in mouth-breathers with mild sleep apnea suggesting possible benefit, and conclude that demonstrated benefit is minimal. The main concerns are taping over nasal obstruction or undiagnosed sleep apnea, skin irritation and suffocation anxiety. Clinicians advise that people with snoring, daytime sleepiness or blocked nasal airways be evaluated before trying it.
deepLead:
Mouth taping is the practice of placing a strip of tape, a porous patch or a similar adhesive over the lips during sleep to keep the mouth closed and encourage breathing through the nose. It spread widely through social media, where it has been credited with benefits ranging from better sleep, less snoring and fresher breath to improved immunity, dental health and energy.
Published research is sparse. A 2025 systematic review located ten studies with 213 patients in total and found that two reported statistically significant improvement in sleep apnea markers, while others found no difference. A scoping review found nine eligible studies and likewise noted that only two reported significant improvements in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) metrics. Authors of these reviews and of accompanying commentaries have called for more rigorous trials and discussed safety questions, particularly for people with nasal obstruction or undiagnosed sleep-disordered breathing.
In looksmaxxing contexts, mouth taping is sometimes linked to the idea that nasal breathing and a closed-mouth posture influence facial structure. The reviews cited here evaluated sleep and breathing outcomes and did not assess facial shape.

name: Mewing appliances

angle.text: Users buy palate plates and mouthpieces alongside mewing, hoping to remodel the jaw, chin and midface. Orthotropic theory is contested; adult skeletal change without orthodontic treatment is undocumented, and the real effect in teens is described as small.

summary: Marketed for palate/jaw remodeling. No adult skeletal change without real orthodontic treatment.
currentQuick:
Mewing appliances are palate-expanding or tongue-posture devices, including mouthpieces and plates, sold to supplement the practice of mewing, in which the tongue is held against the roof of the mouth in the hope of remodeling the jaw and midface. The practice comes from orthotropics, developed by John Mew.
It is a central idea in looksmaxxing forums, where users seek a more forward jaw, higher cheekbones and a sharper jawline.
How it works: The theory is that sustained tongue pressure on the palate changes how facial bones grow. This is considered plausible in growing children with proper orthodontic appliances, but no controlled evidence of skeletal change in adults from tongue posture or over-the-counter appliances has been published.
Risks and caveats: No randomized trials or controlled studies of mewing in adults were found; orthodontic bodies say there is no reliable evidence it reshapes the jaw. Forcing a tongue posture or wearing ill-fitting appliances can strain the jaw joint, shift teeth or cause discomfort. Myofunctional therapy supervised by a clinician has modest support for specific conditions such as sleep-disordered breathing, which is a different claim. The scholarly links listed are the closest relevant research identified, not studies of mewing itself.
deepLead:
Mewing appliances are oral devices, including palate-expanding plates, mouthpieces and tongue-posture aids, marketed to accompany 'mewing', the practice of resting the whole tongue against the roof of the mouth with the lips sealed and breathing through the nose. Mewing is named after the British orthodontist John Mew and belongs to orthotropics, his theory that tongue, lip and breathing posture guide facial growth.
Proponents claim sustained correct posture can produce a more forward jaw, sharper jawline and improved midface and airway. Orthodontic organisations cited in an encyclopedic summary state that mewing cannot reliably reshape the jaw or correct bite problems, and the American Association of Orthodontists has cautioned against forcing unnatural tongue positions. A 2019 article in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery examined mewing as a social media alternative to orthognathic surgery, and a 2026 piece in the Journal of Clinical Orthodontics addressed the trend.
No randomized or controlled trial of over-the-counter mewing appliances in adults has been published in the sources reviewed here. The closest research concerns clinician-supervised orthodontic and orthotropic treatment, mostly in children, and case reports in adults.

name: Red light LED mask

chain: Red light absorbed by skin cells
angle.text: Users wear red light masks to smooth fine lines, even tone, calm acne and improve texture. It is one of the better-studied consumer device categories, though trials vary by device; claims about hair loss or focus and household red lamps are weaker.

summary: Photobiomodulation for fine lines, tone, and texture — one of the few device categories with decent trial data.
currentQuick:
A red light LED mask is a wearable panel that emits red and often near-infrared light, typically around 630 to 850 nanometers, against the face for several minutes at a time. It is a home version of low-level light therapy used in dermatology clinics.
It is marketed for fine lines, skin tone and texture, and post-procedure recovery, and is one of the better-studied home beauty device categories.
How it works: Red and near-infrared light is absorbed by mitochondrial enzymes such as cytochrome c oxidase in skin cells, which is thought to boost cellular energy and stimulate fibroblasts to make collagen while reducing inflammation. This process is called photobiomodulation.
Risks and caveats: Eye exposure is the main safety concern, so goggles or closed eyes are advised, and mild warmth or redness is possible. Sham-controlled trials show modest improvements in crow's feet and skin elasticity, but studies are small, often short and sometimes industry sponsored, and devices vary widely in dose and wavelength. Effects fade if treatment stops, and reported results are subtle.
deepLead:
A red light LED mask is a wearable or handheld panel that delivers red light, and often near-infrared light, to the face for a few minutes per session. The technology is a consumer form of low-level light therapy, also called photobiomodulation (PBM), which applies low-power lasers or LEDs without damaging tissue. Typical marketed wavelengths fall in the red (about 620-700 nm) and near-infrared (about 700-1440 nm) ranges.
Masks are sold for fine lines, skin tone and texture, and recovery after procedures. A 2024 dermatology continuing-education review states that PBM is used effectively for conditions including acne, skin rejuvenation, wounds, scars and alopecia and describes it as having a favourable safety profile. Home-device trials are fewer; a multicentre, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled study of a home LED and infrared mask for crow's feet was published in 2025, and a split-face pilot of a 637 and 854 nm home LED device appeared in 2020.
Reviewers note that devices vary widely in wavelength and dose, and that trial sizes are modest and sometimes industry-linked.
